summary: Specifies SDP signalling that identifies the reference clock source used for NTP-format timestamps and the media clock sources in a multimedia session.

eli5.summary: Different devices need to know which clock to look at to stay together. This gives a way to say which clock is the boss.

questions: what is rtp clock source signalling
what does ts-refclk mean in sdp
subtitle: SDP attributes that say which clock a media stream's timestamps and sample timing are tied to.

tldr.problem: RTP implementations usually assume NTP timestamps come from unsynchronised clocks, so tight synchronisation between receivers or between senders is not possible, and there is no standard way to say which clocks are shared.
tldr.mechanism: Two SDP attributes, ts-refclk and mediaclk, identify the timestamp reference clock (NTP, PTP, GPS-style, private or local) and how the media clock is derived (sender, direct from the reference, or from a master stream).
tldr.outcome: Devices can check whether they share a clock before joining a session, enabling applications such as video walls and networked audio, but the signalled values can be forged and should not be used as a secure time source.

today: RFC 7273 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It remains the definition of the ts-refclk and mediaclk SDP attributes.

sections.title: The Clock Problem in RTP
sections.content:
RTP protocols use NTP format timestamps to synchronise multimedia sessions and to estimate round-trip time. The clock behind those timestamps may be synchronised to a global time reference, but this cannot be assumed, and there is no standard way to indicate that timestamps come from a common reference clock. So RTP implementations typically assume the clocks are unsynchronised and compensate for time and rate differences.

Without a shared reference clock, RTP can align flows from one source at one receiver using relative timing. Tight synchronisation between different receivers, or between several senders, is not possible.

High performance audio and video systems often distribute a separate reference media clock to all devices, for example genlock or an audio word clock. If sending and receiving media clocks are known to share a reference, performance improves by minimising buffering and avoiding rate conversion. RFC 7273 defines SDP signalling for both the timestamp reference clock and the media clock.
sections.eli5: If every kid in a relay race has a different watch, nobody agrees who was fastest. This RFC lets everyone say which watch they are using.

sections.title: Who Needs Shared Clocks
sections.content:
The RFC lists applications that need synchronised capture or playout and low latency:

  • Social TV: friends watching the same broadcast in different places, where one seeing a goal well before another spoils the experience.
  • Video walls: several screens tiled into one large picture, which only works if their refreshes are synchronised.
  • Networked audio: loudspeakers, amplifiers and I/O devices around a building. Humans are sensitive to audio delay, so the accuracy needed can be in the range of microseconds.
  • Sensor arrays: sonar, seismic and radar arrays, where the phase relationship between element signals is critical.
sections.eli5: A video wall made of many screens only looks like one big picture if every screen changes at exactly the same moment.

sections.title: Timestamp Reference Clocks
sections.content:
A sender or receiver takes NTP format timestamps from a local real-time clock, which may be synchronised to a time source by NTP, PTP or a radio clock such as GPS. To serve as a reference clock, clocks must minimally be syntonised, meaning exactly frequency matched. The accuracy needed depends on the application.

The RFC defines these kinds of source:

  • NTP: a server named by host name or IP address and an optional port, with 123 assumed if omitted. Several servers listed at one level are interchangeable.
  • PTP: IEEE 1588-2002, IEEE 1588-2008 or IEEE 802.1AS-2011. A clock is identified by the 64-bit ClockIdentity (an EUI-64) of the grandmaster plus a domain. Senders and receivers SHOULD check that both the grandmaster and the domain match.
  • Global clocks: GPS, Galileo and GLONASS, identified by name alone.
  • Private: some other source, such as digital television or cellular time, whose equivalence is checked by means outside this RFC.
  • Local: a local wallclock, assumed equivalent only to clocks in the same device.
  • Traceable: any clock proven synchronised to International Atomic Time (TAI). Marking a source traceable lets the SDP omit addresses, so an offer of ts-refclk:ntp=/traceable/ can be answered using GPS.
sections.eli5: Some clocks come from a time server, some from satellites, and some are just a device's own watch. The description names which kind everyone should check against.

sections.title: The ts-refclk Attribute
sections.content:
The reference clock is signalled with a=ts-refclk:<clksrc>. It may appear at session level, media level or source level (as a=ssrc:<ssrc-id> ts-refclk:<clksrc>). Session level sets defaults for everything; media level overrides session level; source level overrides media level. If signalling appears anywhere in a description it must be properly defined for all levels, which is easy to do with a session-level default.

The attribute may be repeated at one level to list more clocks, and all clocks at that level are assumed equivalent. Traceable sources MUST NOT be mixed with non-traceable ones at the same level. Clock details can change, for example after a PTP grandmaster election, and SIP supports re-signalling updated SDP, while other protocols may need other notification mechanisms.

PTP domains are written as a name (IEEE 1588-2002, up to 16 characters) or a number (IEEE 1588-2008, 0 to 127).
sections.eli5: You can write the "boss clock" on the whole session, or on one stream. A note on a single stream wins over the note on the whole session.

sections.title: Media Clock Sources
sections.content:
The media clock sets the timebase that advances RTP timestamps. The mediaclk attribute describes three modes.

  • Asynchronous (sender): the sender samples with a free-running local clock. This is the assumed mode when nothing is signalled.
  • Direct-referenced (direct): the media clock is derived straight from a reference clock, so a ts-refclk is required. An optional offset gives the RTP timestamp value at the reference clock's epoch, and streams using an offset SHOULD use a TAI reference to avoid leap-second complications. Without an offset, the receiver infers the mapping from RTCP sender reports, which take precedence, though the rate they imply MUST agree with the signalled one. An optional rate ratio of two integers adjusts the clock rate, mainly for the odd audio sample rates associated with NTSC video.
  • Stream-referenced: a master device's media clock is identified by a base64 master clock identifier, which SHOULD be generated with the short-term persistent RTCP CNAME algorithm of RFC 7022. The master stream is tagged with a src: prefix, and slaved senders include the same identifier. An IEEE 1722 stream can be named with mediaclk:IEEE1722=<StreamID>.

Slaving a media clock to a master does not change RTP inter-media synchronisation, which still relies on NTP timestamps from RTCP sender reports or the RFC 6051 header extension.
sections.eli5: A musician can play to their own beat, follow the big clock on the wall, or copy the drummer. The description says which of the three they are doing.

sections.title: Signalling and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
A description SHOULD include both reference clock and media clock signalling. With no media clock signalling, an asynchronous media clock MUST be assumed; with no reference clock signalling, a local reference clock MUST be assumed. A direct-referenced media clock REQUIRES reference clock signalling. A party with nothing specific to signal SHOULD include a local reference clock to show it supports the feature.

In the SDP offer/answer model the signalling is declarative. The offer lists supported clocks, and the answerer may accept it, fall back to a lower-performance mode, or reject it when the clocks are incompatible. An answerer SHOULD reply with the subset of offered reference clocks it can use. A rejection MUST include at least one usable reference clock specification for diagnostics. Negotiation itself is not defined here but MAY use the capability negotiation of RFC 5939.

Outside offer/answer, for example sessions announced with SAP or streamed with RTSP, devices SHOULD check their synchronisation compatibility and SHOULD NOT join a session whose clocks are incompatible.
sections.eli5: Before joining a game, you check whether you have the same kind of clock as the host. If you do not, you can play a simpler version or say no.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A session description cannot be trusted unless it came over an authenticated transport from a known source. Wrong clock parameters can make devices synchronise to unintended sources. Usually that only causes a failed session or failed synchronisation, but enough devices falsely assigned to one clock source, such as a particular IEEE 1588 grandmaster, could amount to a denial-of-service attack on it. Devices MAY validate the clock description before connecting to unfamiliar sources.

The negotiated reference clocks provide media timing for RTP. They should not be relied on as a secure time reference for security-critical operations such as certificate expiry.
sections.eli5: If someone hands you a fake note saying which clock to follow, you might follow the wrong one. And a clock chosen only to keep music in time should not be used to decide whether a password has expired.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: RFC 7273 registers the SDP attributes ts-refclk and mediaclk (session, media and source level). It also creates two sub-registries under the IANA SDP Parameters registry: the Timestamp Reference Clock Source Parameters registry, with the initial names ntp, ptp, gps, gal, glonass, local and private, and the Media Clock Source Parameters registry, with sender, direct and IEEE1722. Future assignments in both use the Specification Required policy.
sections.eli5: There are two official lists, one of clock kinds and one of ways to follow a clock, and new entries need a written specification.
